design_detail: Essay (PLoS Medicine's Essay section, described there as opinion pieces) built on a simple probability model, by a single author, with no new data and nothing specific to drugs. A 'research finding' is any relationship reaching formal statistical significance. From a 2 × 2 table of claimed findings against true relationships the essay derives the positive predictive value (PPV: the probability, after a study, that a claimed finding is true) from the pre-study odds R that a probed relationship is true, the power (1 − β) and the significance level α (0.05); then adds a bias term u (the share of analyses that would not have been findings but are reported as such because of design, data, analysis or presentation factors) and n independent teams testing the same question (pp. 696–698; Tables 1–3). Six corollaries follow. Table 4 gives PPVs for nine author-chosen combinations of power, R and u, each labelled with a 'practical example' of a design; Box 1 works an example of a genome-wide association study; Figures 1 and 2 plot PPV against R for power 0.20, 0.50 and 0.80 at several levels of u and n (pp. 698–700).
can_establish: That, under the stated model, the probability that a statistically significant finding is true depends on the pre-study odds, power, bias and the number of teams testing the same question, can fall well below one half, and changes in the stated directions with each of these.
cannot_establish: The actual share of false findings in any field (the inputs R, u and power are assumed, not measured, and the examples assign them without data); whether any given finding is true; or anything specific to drug research, which the essay does not discuss.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable: no participants and no data. The model's inputs are assumed values; empirical support is cited from the literature (refutations across designs, genetic association studies, microarrays, selective outcome reporting in trials, rapidly alternating contradictory results called the Proteus phenomenon, contradicted highly cited clinical research), 8 of the 37 references being the author's own (pp. 696–701).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable. The essay considers relationships that investigators claim exist, not null findings (p. 696).
sample.selection_effects: The nine scenarios of Table 4 and the example of Box 1 were chosen by the author, with no stated basis for the values of R and u given to each design (p. 700; Box 1, p. 699).

comparison.controls: None. Scenarios are compared with one another (Table 4; Figures 1 and 2).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. The analogue is the unmeasured inputs: no field's pre-study odds or bias is estimated.

outcomes.instruments: Algebra from 2 × 2 tables: PPV = (1 − β)R/(R − βR + α) without bias; PPV = ([1 − β]R + uβR)/(R + α − βR + u − uα + uβR) with bias; PPV = R(1 − β^n)/(R + 1 − [1 − α]^n − Rβ^n) for n independent studies of equal power (pp. 696–697; Tables 1–3, pp. 697–698).
outcomes.validity_norms: The model's predictions are not tested against observed replication or refutation rates; the essay states that the assumptions about pre-study odds needed to apply it would be considerably subjective (p. 701).
outcomes.operationalization: A finding is 'true' if the probed relationship exists and 'false' otherwise (truth is binary; effect size enters only through power); a research finding is any relationship claimed on the basis of P < α (p. 696). 'Most findings are false' corresponds to PPV < 0.5.

analysis.effect_sizes: Not applicable (no data). Printed model results: a finding is more likely true than false if (1 − β)R > α, that is (1 − β)R > 0.05 at α = 0.05 (pp. 696–697). Table 4 (p. 700), power, R and u with the author's example and PPV: 0.80, 1:1, 0.10, adequately powered RCT with little bias, 0.85; 0.95, 2:1, 0.30, confirmatory meta-analysis of good-quality RCTs, 0.85; 0.80, 1:3, 0.40, meta-analysis of small inconclusive studies, 0.41; 0.20, 1:5, 0.20, underpowered but well-performed phase I/II RCT, 0.23; 0.20, 1:5, 0.80, underpowered, poorly performed phase I/II RCT, 0.17; 0.80, 1:10, 0.30, adequately powered exploratory epidemiological study, 0.20; 0.20, 1:10, 0.30, underpowered exploratory epidemiological study, 0.12; 0.20, 1:1,000, 0.80, discovery-oriented exploratory research with massive testing, 0.0010; 0.20, 1:1,000, 0.20, the same with more limited bias, 0.0015. Box 1 (p. 699): R = 10^-4 and power 0.60 give a PPV of 12 × 10^-4 without bias, 4.4 × 10^-4 with u = 0.10, and 1.5 × 10^-4 when ten teams test and one finds significance. Editors' recalculation from the printed bias formula reproduces all nine PPVs of Table 4 and the first two Box 1 values; the ten-team value does not follow from the printed formula (reporting issues).
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable in the usual sense; the scenarios shown were chosen by the author.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A conditional result: under the model, significant findings are more likely false than true whenever power times pre-study odds is below α (0.05), and bias, small studies, small effects, many tested relationships, flexible analyses, conflicts of interest and many competing teams lower the probability further. In seven of the nine illustrative scenarios chosen by the author the PPV is below 0.5; in the two describing adequately powered trials and confirmatory meta-analyses it is 0.85.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title, the summary and a pull-quote present the conclusion as general and proven: the pull-quote says it “can be proven that most claimed research findings are false” (p. 696), and the summary says that simulations show it for most designs and settings (p. 696). What is proven is the formula; whether most real fields have the low pre-study odds, low power and bias that push the PPV below one half is asserted (the majority of modern biomedical research is said to work in areas of very low pre- and post-study probability, p. 700) but not shown with data, and the 'simulations' are calculations for nine author-chosen scenarios (pp. 699–700). Near its end the essay concedes that the assumptions needed would be considerably subjective (p. 701).

timeline.event: A large replication project in psychology cites the essay (its ref. 9) and finds 35 of 97 significant findings significant again on one replication, while warning that a failed replication does not show the original finding was false

replication.where_it_stands: A model, not a finding, so not replicable as such; its premises are tested by replication studies. The one read alongside it found low reproducibility in three psychology journals, consistent with the essay's warning, although non-replication is not the same as falsehood (Open Science Collaboration, 2015, pp. aac4716-4, aac4716-6). Provisional: no published critique or re-analysis of the model was read for this card.

funding.declared_conflicts: The author has declared that no competing interests exist (p. 696).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Hygiene and Epidemiology, University of Ioannina School of Medicine, Greece, and Institute for Clinical Research and Health Policy Studies, Tufts-New England Medical Center, Boston (p. 696). 8 of the 37 references are the author's own (refs 1, 5, 7, 8, 19, 29, 30, 36), including several of the empirical examples (p. 701).

what_would_settle_it: Field-by-field estimates of the share of published significant findings that hold up, from large preregistered replications of random samples of published findings, together with empirical estimates of power, bias and pre-study odds against which the model's predictions could be checked.

domains.domain: Model assumptions and their empirical support
domains.note: The inputs that drive the conclusion (pre-study odds R, bias u, power) are assumed; the values in Table 4 and Box 1 come without data or sources (pp. 699–700). Simplifications are stated: one significance level, binary truth, bias independent of truth, and fields with one true relationship or equal power for all (pp. 696–697).

domains.domain: Comparison with the phenomenon it explains
domains.note: The model's predictions are not compared with any observed rate of replication or refutation; the supporting evidence is cited, not analysed (pp. 696, 698–699).

domains.domain: Sensitivity of the conclusions to parameter choices
domains.note: Figures 1 and 2 show how the PPV varies with R, power, u and n (pp. 698–699), so sensitivity is displayed; the general claim about most findings depends on where real fields lie in that space, which is not examined.
All formulas and inputs are printed; the editors reproduced all nine PPVs of Table 4 and the first two Box 1 values. The third Box 1 value does not follow from the printed formula (reporting issues).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own work
domains.note: 8 of 37 references are the author's, among them the main empirical examples of refutation (genetic associations, microarrays, the Proteus phenomenon, contradicted highly cited clinical research) (pp. 696–701).

The pull-quote and summary present a conditional calculation as proof of a general fact (p. 696), and the claim that most modern biomedical research works at very low pre-study odds is asserted (p. 700). Elsewhere speculation is flagged, for example the author's suspicion that several established classics will fail the test (p. 701).

domains.domain: Balance (what raises the probability that a finding is true)
domains.note: The several-teams model covers only the case where at least one of n teams finds significance, which lowers the PPV; consistent findings by several independent teams, which would raise it, are not modelled, though large studies, low-bias meta-analyses and the totality of the evidence are named as remedies (pp. 697, 700–701).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument exists for a theoretical essay (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is applied with domains suited to models, as on other modelling cards. The algebra is simple, correct and transparent, and Table 4 reproduces exactly. The weakness is the step from the model to the title: the inputs are assumed, so the essay shows how published findings can be mostly false, not that they are. The card may be cited for the framework (the probability that a significant finding is true depends on pre-study odds, power, bias and the number of teams; small studies, small effects, many tested relationships, flexible designs and analyses, financial and other interests and hot fields lower it), for its point that statistical significance in a single study does not by itself make a finding probably true, and for its numbers as illustrations under stated assumptions. It may not be cited as a measured proportion of false findings in any field, drug research included.

key_findings.finding: Model result: at α = 0.05 a statistically significant finding is more likely true than false only if power times the pre-study odds exceeds 0.05 ((1 − β)R > α), so whether a significant result is probably true depends on the prior odds and the power, not on the P value alone (editors' illustration from this formula: with 80% power the pre-study odds must exceed 1 to 16, a prior probability of about 6%).
key_findings.locator: Modeling the Framework for False Positive Findings, 2nd paragraph (starts p. 696, ends p. 697); Table 1 (p. 697)
key_findings.note: Bears on the plain reading of 'significant' as 'probably not chance': in this model a result with P < 0.05 can still be more likely false than true when pre-study odds or power are low, or bias is present.

key_findings.finding: The author calls it ill-founded to claim conclusive findings from a single study judged only by formal statistical significance (typically P < 0.05), and says research is not best represented and summarized by P values.
key_findings.locator: Modeling the Framework for False Positive Findings, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: With bias u the PPV falls as u rises (unless power is no greater than α); with n independent teams of equal power, the PPV of a significant finding by any one of them tends to fall as n rises, so a single positive result among many teams' attempts is weaker evidence than it looks.
key_findings.locator: Bias, 1st paragraph; Testing by Several Independent Teams (p. 697); Tables 2 and 3 (pp. 697–698)

key_findings.finding: Six corollaries: a finding is less likely to be true the smaller the studies; the smaller the effect sizes (relative risks of 1.1–1.5 for genetic risk factors for multigenetic diseases, against 3–20 for smoking and cancer or cardiovascular disease); the greater the number and the lesser the preselection of tested relationships; the greater the flexibility in designs, definitions, outcomes and analyses; the greater the financial and other interests and prejudices; and the hotter the field, with more teams involved.

Table 4 (nine author-chosen scenarios, α = 0.05): PPV 0.85 for an adequately powered RCT with little bias and 1:1 pre-study odds, and for a confirmatory meta-analysis of good-quality RCTs; 0.41 for a meta-analysis of small inconclusive studies; 0.23 and 0.17 for underpowered phase I/II RCTs, well or poorly performed; 0.20 and 0.12 for adequately powered and underpowered exploratory epidemiological studies; 0.0010 and 0.0015 for discovery-oriented research with massive testing.
key_findings.locator: Most Research Findings Are False for Most Research Designs and for Most Fields (p. 699); Table 4 (p. 700)
key_findings.note: Editors' recalculation from the printed bias formula reproduces all nine values; the inputs are assumptions, so the PPVs are illustrations, not estimates.

key_findings.finding: Box 1: for a genome-wide association study testing 100,000 polymorphisms of which about ten are truly associated (R = 10^-4), with 60% power, a result just crossing P = 0.05 raises the probability of truth about 12-fold, to only 12 × 10^-4; with bias u = 0.10 it is 4.4 × 10^-4; and when ten teams test and one finds a significant result, 1.5 × 10^-4.
key_findings.note: The ten-team value does not follow from the essay's own formula for n studies (editors' calculation: about 2.5 × 10^-4; reporting issues); either way it stays close to the pre-study probability of 10^-4.

key_findings.finding: In a field with no true effects (a 'null field'), the essay argues, claimed effect sizes measure only the net bias; it illustrates this with a hypothetical literature claiming that 60 nutrients change the risk of a tumour with relative risks of 1.2 to 1.4, and argues that very large and very highly significant effects may more often signal large bias than important discoveries.
key_findings.locator: Claimed Research Findings May Often Be Simply Accurate Measures of the Prevailing Bias, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Remedies proposed: better-powered evidence (large studies, low-bias meta-analyses) aimed at questions with already high pre-study odds; judging the totality of the evidence rather than any single team's significant finding; registration of studies and adherence to protocols; and estimating the pre-study odds before running an experiment. The essay also warns that very large studies may find formally significant differences for trivial effects.
key_findings.locator: How Can We Improve the Situation?, 2nd to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The essay concedes that the assumptions about pre-study odds needed to interpret claims would be considerably subjective, while arguing that they would still help put research claims in context.
key_findings.locator: How Can We Improve the Situation?, last paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Box 1's ten-team value (1.5 × 10^-4) does not follow from the essay's own formula for n independent studies (Testing by Several Independent Teams; Table 3); editors' calculation: with R = 10^-4, power 0.60, α = 0.05 and n = 10 that formula gives about 2.5 × 10^-4, and 1.5 × 10^-4 results only if the single-study power replaces 1 − β^n in the numerator.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor numerically, and the conclusion that the probability stays close to the pre-study value holds either way; but the printed figure should not be quoted as a result of the model.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the cell for a claimed finding without a true relationship is printed as cα + uc(1 − α)/(R + 1), without the brackets that the row total and the PPV formula in the text require: (cα + uc(1 − α))/(R + 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the PPV formula in the text is correct and reproduces Table 4.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary and the text call Table 4 the results of simulations, but its values are direct evaluations of the bias formula for nine chosen parameter sets (editors' recalculation reproduces all nine).
reporting_issues.consequence: 'Simulations show' overstates the evidential basis; the figures illustrate the formula and are not estimates from data.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record, PLoS Medicine 2(8): e124, August 2005), all 6 pages, printed 0696–0701 and cited as pp. 696–701; formulas, Tables 1–4 and Box 1 checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi, and the Table 4 and Box 1 values recalculated from the printed formulas (editors' calculation); the curves of Figures 1 and 2 described, values not extracted. No supplement among the files.
